en: In the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Shi Dunlun Jizhuan Lunben* (The Collected Explanations of the Treatise by Shi Dunlun),

regarding the "Abiding in Higher Ethics" (*adhiśīla-vihāra*), there is first the question, second the explanation, and finally the concluding explanation that reconciles the names. Within the explanation:
There are three [parts].
First is the explanation of the ten intentions (*daśāśaya*),
which the *Dilun* school calls the "initiating pure portion" (*pravṛtti-viśuddhi-bhāga*).
Second, the analysis of the characteristics of abiding;
in that treatise, this is called the "portion of intrinsic purity.
Third, the analysis of comparative evaluation.
In the *Dilun* [commentary], because it uses later sections as precedents, this passage does not appear.
If one follows the concluding text below, there are nine sections;
the subsequent stages likewise follow their respective concluding texts.
This can be understood by dividing it into several sections and comparing them accordingly.
Because the ten types of aspiration (*āśaya*) practiced in the first stage (*bhūmi*) are utterly perfected, one transcends into the second stage.
Among the ten types of intention (*āśaya*), the first nine pertain to self-benefit and the last one to benefiting others.
It is precisely by means of these ten types of intention that [the bodhicitta] becomes of the highest degree;
thus, from "equal" (*sama*) onwards, the second section clarifies the purity of its essential nature (*svabhāva-viśuddhi*).
Within this, the first part clarifies the essence of abiding;
the second part, beginning with "In this abiding," clarifies the characteristics of abiding, which consist of five statements in total.
The first two statements clarify the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).
Next, one phrase clarifies the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
The final two phrases clarify the morality of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
Regarding the statement, "In this abiding, the natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*) is fully possessed":
Although intentional transgressions are absent in the first stage, there are still accidental ones;
now, in the second stage, both intentional and accidental transgressions are entirely absent, and thus it is complete.
This constitutes one phrase.
Second, even the slightest evil transgressions of the precepts do not exist, let alone those of middling or superior degree;
thus, they are free from the stains of violating the precepts.
Third, regarding the manifestation of the ten types of perfect paths of action, and so forth.

This means that because one is able to eliminate the ten paths of unwholesome action, the nature of the ten paths of wholesome action manifests in its full perfection. Thus, being endowed with natural ethical discipline (*śīla*),

one is able, through sublime wisdom, to understand as they truly are the various karmas— both worldly, whether defiled or undefiled— and their results, namely the ripened fruits (*vipākaphala*) and the concordant outflows (*niṣyandaphala*), as well as the concordant outflows of supramundane karma.
The fourth is to personally sever evil and cultivate goodness while further exhorting others to do the same.
The fifth is to impartially contemplate sentient beings and take pity on their suffering;
the "ultimate truth" (paramārtha) suffering here refers to the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
These bodhisattvas abide in the third stage, "The Subtle" (Sūkṣma).
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the analysis of the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
The subsequent section distinguishes the fruition of retribution (*vipākaphala*).
As for the fruition of progress (*nairyāṇikaphala*), since it is subsumed under the fruition of vision (*darśanaphala*) and is restricted to the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is not discussed here.
This follows the interpretation of Master Zhengfa.
Because one practices correct conduct in order to manifest the skillful means for not becoming confused regarding the path, the fruit of setting forth is excluded.
Furthermore, it is not mentioned because it follows the same pattern as the preceding [stages].
According to principle, all ten stages possess the fruit of setting forth.
The fruit of aspiration is identical to that of the first stage;
since it does not differ from what preceded, it is not discussed here.
Within the fruit of pliancy, the text first provides a general indication that it is the same as before.
Later, an analogy is raised to clarify this.

Regarding the statement, "One should know that the purity of the roots of goodness from having extensively seen the Buddhas is as previously described," this refers to what was said earlier in the first bhūmi:
That is to say: because of making offerings to and supporting the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
because of maturing sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);
because of dedicating all roots of goodness toward enlightenment (*bodhi*), and so forth.
To illustrate this through an analogy, first the metaphor is presented and then it is applied to the subject.
*Kāsisa* refers to blue-black alum;
the older treatises refer to it as the medicinal substance *kāśīsa*.
The *Dilun* states that alum stone is used because the substance of gold contains subtle impurities, which are removed by placing it in alum stone.
Within this dwelling, the following section distinguishes the fruition of retribution (*vipākaphala*).
First, the fruit of the householder is explained;
next, the statement "one should know that its power exceeds the former tenfold" indicates the fruit of the renunciant.
As the Old Treatise says:
The ten matters of supernormal power are as explained in the *Sūtra*.
According to the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*,
first, within a single moment of thought, one attains one thousand samādhis, and so on up to twelve thousand.
In each individual body, one can manifest a thousand bodhisattvas as a retinue.
Regarding the phrase "tenfold" used herein:
at the first stage (bhūmi), one attains a hundred.
In the second bhūmi, one attains a thousand;
therefore, the previous claim that it refers to "ten matters" is erroneous.
There is an interpretation [to this effect].
This statement that "power" (*prabhāva*) is synonymous with the "fruit of knowing through aspiration" (*praṇidhijñānaphala*) is not correct according to our current interpretation.
In the concluding explanation that reconciles the names, there are three parts.
The first section provides a concise summary;
the second points to the detailed exposition in the sutra;
and the final section explains and reconciles variant names.
Of the nine phrases in the preceding section,
the first phrase summarizes the ten intentions,
and the following two phrases summarize the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).
Next, there is one phrase that summarizes the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
Next, there are two phrases that summarize the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).
Finally, there is one phrase that summarizes the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-phala*).
Thereafter, there are two lines that conclude by summarizing the fruit of retribution.
Within the "Abiding in the Superior Mind" (*adhi-citta-vihāra*), there is likewise a question-and-answer summary;
within the answer, there are nine lines.
According to the *Yidi lun* (Treatise on the Stages),
the first phrase refers to the entry into the second stage (*bhūmi*) as the skillful means for proceeding to the third stage;
the subsequent phrase refers to the mind of the initial dwelling stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
The next phrase refers to the mind of the stage of the true state (*samyaktva-avasthā*).
The subsequent six phrases clarify the revulsion toward the fruit, which constitutes the mind of the stage's fulfillment (*bhūmi-paripūrṇa-citta*).
Regarding the first of these phrases, it says: "Having already attained the ten kinds of pure intention (*viśuddha-āśaya*)."
Regarding the practice of the self-benefit portion within the second bhūmi,
it is further clarified by means of the remaining ten purities of mind as the superior progress of the second bhūmi,
continuing until one enters the abiding in the higher resolve (*adhyāśaya-vihāra*).
These ten purities of mind are explained according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
First is the purity of profound mindfulness arising in dependence upon that,
as the sūtra says, "because of the pure mind."
Second, relying on not abandoning one's own vehicle,
as the sūtra says, "because the mind is unshakable.
Third, giving rise to skillful means regarding the aspiration for the supreme Dharma.
This is able to bring about revulsion toward future sensual desire,
as the sutra says, "because of a mind of revulsion.
Fourth, based on the sensual desires manifested by others, one is without greed.
As the sūtra says, "because of being free from desire.
Fifth, it relies on not abandoning the benefit of one's own vehicle's path;
as the sūtra says, "because of the non-retrogressive mind."
Sixth, it cannot be destroyed by the afflictions of its own level,
as the sūtra says, "because of a firm mind.
Seventh, it relies on mastery over meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
As the sūtra clarifies, this is because of a "radiant mind.
Eighth, by relying on the sovereign power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), although one may be born in a lower realm, one does not fall away from it;
as the sūtra states, this is because of a "pure mind" (*śuddha-citta*).
Ninth, although afflictions arise based upon them, they cannot defile him;
as the Sūtra says, "because his mind is joyful.
Tenth, he does not sever his existence within the various realms of being (*bhava*) in order to benefit sentient beings.
As stated in the Sūtra, "Because of the great mind," this section is judged according to that treatise;
this concludes the explanation of the "Section on the Practice of Approaching."
Next, there is one phrase that clarifies the mind of the initial stage of dwelling:
it refers to the bodhisattva’s abiding [in the stage] up until the point where they are able to give rise to a vast and great compassionate intention (*āśaya*).
That is to say, when the bodhisattva dwells in the "dwelling of the superior mind" (*adhyāśaya-vihāra*).

All various kinds of faults and afflictions that can destroy all virtuous practices—[the practitioner] is able to develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.
This is what is meant by "generating a mind that takes the meaning of dependent origination as its object."
This refers to the mind that intends to bring about benefit and happiness;
"intention" (artha) here means the sense of benefiting.
The subsequent phrase clarifies the mind that abides in the ground.
This refers to the causal sequence beginning from the contemplation of all sentient beings up until their hearing of the true Dharma.
Within this, the initial contemplation of the means for sentient beings to be liberated from suffering is exclusively the unobstructed wisdom of the Buddha.
Next, one infers that the Buddha’s wisdom arises from the non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) produced through that training;
next, one infers that this wisdom arises by relying on meditative concentration (samādhi),
namely the concentrations and so forth cultivated in the third stage (bhūmi).
Furthermore, by inferring this, one knows with certainty that [this realization] arises from the teaching, preceded by hearing.
Having observed this, there follow six phrases which constitute the fruit of the stage of revulsion.
First, seeking the true Dharma without weariness;
second, from "having initiated such diligence as a bodhisattva" onwards, being able to correctly practice the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*);

third, from "having dwelt extensively [in meditative absorption] and then again relinquished it" onwards, relinquishing dhyāna and giving rise to craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) according to one's inclination.

To say that such a bodhisattva is called "one who has severed the fetters of desire" because they have abandoned desire means they have attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through detachment from desire.
To say they are called "one who has severed the fetters of existence" means they have relinquished the dhyānas, samādhis, and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
"Abandoning what is above and not receiving it is called severing the bonds of existence.
Regarding the phrase "first from the stage of practice through conviction until finally becoming non-retrogressive," Jing says:

Having first entered the contemplation of *tathatā* from the stage of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-bhūmi*), the fetters of views and the perverse greed, hatred, and delusion are severed and never again arise.
Tai states:
"This is because, from the stage of practice through resolute conviction, one cultivates resolute conviction regarding the *tathatā* of phenomena."
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-bandhana*) have already been severed;
the false greed, hatred, and delusion arising in dependence upon those fetters of views are likewise extinguished accordingly.
If the conceptualization of a self-view is included within the fetters of views, [it is so].
In the first bhūmi, the seeds are severed entirely.
As for the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātmadṛṣṭi*), which is comprised within the fetters of desire and the fetters of existence, it is suppressed so as not to arise in the fourth bhūmi;
its seeds are finally severed only upon reaching the vajra-like samādhi.
The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) also encompasses both conceptual (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*) types, just as the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) was previously severed.
This is because the two [views]—false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the two graspings (*parāmarśa*)—arise only conceptually.
These three views are subsumed solely under the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*).
The Bodhisattva of the first stage exhausts the seeds [of affliction].
From "Having widely seen the Buddhas" onwards, it clarifies the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Regarding the stages such as "weighing" (*tulana*) and so forth:
The first two stages are like ore that has not yet been fully refined;
though both existences are scorched, they are only slightly lightened.
Now, in the third stage, it is as when the ore is exhausted and the gold is pure.
The seventh explains the certainty of the two abodes;
the eighth explains the taking of birth;
and the ninth explains sovereign power.
This is also a passage concerning the fruit of the maturation of rewards (*vipākaphala*).
Jing says:
"The phrase 'all its majestic power' and following clarifies the fruit of majestic power within the fruit of the wisdom of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*)."
Now, the explanation is not thus.
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the first fetter is explained briefly;
next, the Sūtra is cited for a detailed explanation.
Next, the explanation of alternative names for the assembly:

"By means of the light of the correct Dharma through the practice of hearing and the light of meditative concentration (*samādhi*)," etc., means that when seeking the Dharma, the light of the Dharma is illuminated by the wisdom of hearing;
therefore, it is called "the light of the correct Dharma through the practice of hearing."
Because cultivation arises from hearing, it is said that "the light of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth" [is attained].
Regarding "purity of the inner mind," it means that because one realizes the light of the wisdom of internal cultivation on this stage, it is called "purity of the inner mind."
The untainted or pure mind is called the internal mind;
this refers precisely to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This addresses the question regarding the resolution of bonds within the "Abiding in Superior Wisdom Associated with the Factors of Enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣya-saṃprayukta-adhiprajñā-vihāra*).
Based on the concluding text below, one should know that within this section there are thirteen parts.
Regarding the first part, which states, "That is to say, for all bodhisattvas... up to 'one should know their characteristics,'" this is according to what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
"One should enter the fourth stage by means of ten dharmas of illumination (*dharmāloka-praveśa*). What are these ten? and so on, as explained at length.
The *Dìlùn* (Treatise on the Stages) commentary states:
"Entering by means of the illumination of dharmas" refers to attaining the light of realization regarding the stages.
By means of that wisdom-illumination, one enters into the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata;
that wisdom is called "entry into the illumination of Dharma.
Because one correctly contemplates and deliberates upon what has been taught, knowing it as it truly is, one proceeds in accordance with those two bases.
This reflection has ten types of distinctions.
It is the reflection that discriminates the conventional designations of sentient beings,
as in the sūtra which explains the entry into the illumination of the realm of sentient beings through reflection.
The analysis based on the sūtras is for the purpose of clearly entering the world through contemplation as taught in the sūtras;
the analysis based on defilement is for the purpose of clearly entering the dharma-realm through contemplation as taught in the sūtras;
and the inexhaustible analysis is for the purpose of clearly entering the realm of space through contemplation as taught in the sūtras.
The discrimination regarding the basis of defilement and purity is as explained in the Sūtra through the clear entry into the realm of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).

The discrimination regarding the defilement by latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) is as explained in the Sūtra through the clear entry into the realms of desire, form, and formlessness (*kāma-, rūpa-, and ārūpya-dhātu*).
It is because of the clear entry into the realm of certainty through the superior mind that reflects upon the pure discernment as taught in the sūtras;
it is because of the clear entry into the realm of certainty through the great mind that reflects upon it.
Among these, there are those who are driven by afflictions.
This refers to the three realms.
Regarding the latter two phrases:
first, non-defilement based on afflictions.
Second, regarding the meaning of whether or not [the Bodhisattva] is equal to the Śrāvakas and others in terms of not abandoning sentient beings:
this treatise now states, "If one were to assume...
and so forth. Jing says:
In this context, there are ten dharmas of the "entrances into illumination" (*vairocanāvatāra*) that briefly explain the meaning.
That is to say: first, regarding those which are designations, they are the entrance into illumination;
sentient beings are a mere collection existing by designation.
If it is that which is conceptually designated based upon those [elements], this is the second [kind].
That which is conventionally established as the world abiding in the world is also a collection existing only as a conceptual construct.
If it is by virtue of this third [nature],
namely the defiled phenomena of the three natures such as the contaminated wholesome and so forth,
that sentient beings and the receptacle world are conventionally designated through these factors of the dharma-realm belonging to the three natures.
If the ultimate truth of equality is the fourth,
it is the great space (*mahākāśa*);
for that suchness (*tathatā*) may also be described as being called "space."
Herein, the equality of the ultimate truth is explained.
That which becomes defiled through affliction and becomes purified through purification is the fifth [consciousness],
because consciousness is the locus upon which defilement and purification depend.
It is said that they constitute defilement and purification.
If they are defiled by the afflictions of bondage, these are the sixth, seventh, and eighth [consciousnesses],
because the three realms are established separately based on the distinctions of the bondage of the desire, form, and formless realms through their deliberation.
If that which is purified by the unsurpassed purity refers to the ninth and tenth [stages],
these are the two luminous entries (*prabhāvitāvatāra*) of the superior good and the great good.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) nirvāṇa of the two vehicles is called "superior good" because it is undefiled.
The Mahāyāna is called "greatly virtuous" (*mahā-kuśala*) because it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and surpasses those two vehicles.
Second, to clarify the accomplishment of wisdom:
as stated in the sūtras, from "unwavering intention" (*abhedya-āśaya*) up to "all are fully matured," this is the foremost.
This refers to the ten kinds of dharma-knowledge that can bring about wisdom;
wisdom is that which is accomplished,
and these ten are the dharmas that mature wisdom.
This is the intended meaning here.
Regarding the phrase "having unimpaired intention as the foremost," Master Ki explains:
Because it is the first among the ten dharmas, it is called the "foremost.
The *Dìchí jīng* (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra) states:
"Maturating the unbreakable purities is the foremost."
In the *Bhūmi-sūtra*, the second [topic], "Homage to the Three Jewels," is named "Unbreakable Purity" (*akṣayaprasāda*).
The present explanation corresponds to its first [point], "the non-retrogressive mind.
"Unbreakable" (*akṣaya*) carries the meaning of "non-retrogressive" (*avaivartika*).
The Sūtra says that because it is the initial wisdom, it is called "foremost.
That same Sūtra states:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva has attained the Great Ground (mahābhūmi)."
This is because they turn toward the family of the Tathāgata, gaining power through the attainment of the internal Dharma,
and because they teach and bring others to maturity through ten kinds of knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). What are these ten?
First, because of the non-retrogressive mind;
second, because of relying on the Three Jewels with definitive reverence and ultimate sincerity;
third, because of discerning and contemplating the process of arising and ceasing.
Fourth, by analytically observing that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unarisen;
fifth, by analytically observing the pure wisdom of the world;
sixth, by analytically observing that arising is characterized by suffering.
7. By means of discerning and observing the world and nirvāṇa;
8. By means of discerning and observing the distinctions in the karma of sentient beings and worlds;
9. By means of discerning and observing the distinctions between the prior limit and the subsequent limit.
Because analytical observation is inexhaustible.
To say that one is "long in the family of the Tathāgata" means that the first stage (*bhūmi*) is called being born into the family of the Tathāgata.
Having already been born there, this present stage and others are called "growing in the family of the Tathāgata.
Those who have attained that essential nature (dharmatā) are described in the *Purva-bhūmi-vyavasthāna* as having "attained mastery" (*vaśitā*).
The Sūtra states: "Having attained mastery over the household, one further attains power and sovereignty;
moreover, by attaining the fundamental dharma (tǐfǎ), one attains the essence of the Tathāgata.
This means that true suchness (tathatā) is the fundamental dharma.
Furthermore, regarding the ten masteries (*vaśitā*), which constitute the essence of the dharmas,
the third section distinguishes the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
It states that this is "by virtue of contemplating the sovereign power (*ādhipatya*) of all aspects of the bodhisattva."
This clarifies the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment.
Taking "enlightenment" (bodhi) as the object is what is termed "enlightenment";
it is the objective realm that is sought.
The term *sattva* refers to sentient beings (*sattva*),
who are the objects to be converted;
furthermore, it refers to sentient beings who seek awakening.
Furthermore, "sattva" carries the meaning of "valiant.
It refers to one who valiantly seeks great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
The fourth [point] distinguishes and severs the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
This means that on this stage, one is able to abandon and suppress the view of self within the sixth consciousness,
though other afflictions such as greed and hatred still remain;
it is upon entering the eighth stage that the seventh consciousness is suppressed.
"Because of their abandonment," and so forth, is the fifth section, which clarifies the prohibition of certain actions and the allowance of others,
as well as the distancing from and the cultivation of [certain practices].
"Since it has been thus," and so forth, is the sixth section, which clarifies the taming and softening of the mind.
According to the *Dichilun* (Treatise on the Stages), there are ten types of mind:
first, the moistening and benefiting mind;
second, the warming mind.
Third, the mind that is disciplined;
fourth, the mind of peaceful happiness;
fifth, the undefiled mind.
Sixth, the mind that repeatedly seeks ever-higher and more excellent practices;
seventh, the mind of superior wisdom;
eighth, the mind that seeks worldly [attainments].
Ninth, the mind that respectfully follows and receives instruction from all teachers;
tenth, the mind that practices according to the Dharma as it has been heard.
This treatise contains three phrases.
The first [stage], "moistening and softening," subsumes those first three minds;
furthermore, "moistening" refers to the first mind,
"the moistening benefit," while "softening" refers to the second mind, "warmth."
Harmony is the third [stage] of taming the mind.
Second, being capable of mastery, it comprises that peaceful and blissful state of non-defiled mind.
Third, as the mind further evolves through various modes of activity, it becomes thoroughly purified; this comprises the latter five states of mind.
Furthermore, from the passage "Moreover, he well understands gratitude" onwards, the seventh section clarifies that all qualities of conformity flourish and prosper.
As stated in the *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra):

"This bodhisattva, having thus accomplished a mind of gratitude and a mind of requiting gratitude, becomes increasingly gentle; he dwells in peace and happiness with others, possessing a straightforward mind and a warm heart."
Free from the conduct of dense thickets, without guile or crookedness, and without conceit,
they properly receive instruction and grasp the intention of the speaker.
This treatise cites the first two phrases as representative of the remaining ones.
"Seeking the higher stages until attaining and abiding therein" refers to the eighth branch of the cultivation of the stages, which is great diligence.
The *Bhūmi-sūtra* elucidates ten types of diligence:
first, unceasing diligence;
and so on, up to the tenth, the diligence of skillfully discriminating between what is the path and what is not the path.
As explained extensively therein,
it clarifies the purification of the superior intention and resolute conviction;
the tenth clarifies that the enemies of the holy teaching cannot overwhelm or disturb it.
The *Dì jīng* (Bhūmi-sūtra) states:
"This bodhisattva’s realm of the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*) is pure;
the realm of the profound mind is not lost."
The realm of faith and understanding becomes increasingly clear and sharp;
wholesome roots arise and increase;
and one remains far removed from the defilements and turbidity of the world.
Having severed all doubts, they are free from the net of uncertainty;
they manifest and fully possess matured joy and bliss.
The Tathāgata manifests before them, and their immeasurable profound resolve manifests and reaches maturity.
Now, this text is judged to belong to this present section:
specifically, the passage from "until the roots of goodness have increased" up to "not yet assigned to the ninth phrase" corresponds to the first phrase;
the passage from "having distanced oneself from the defilements of the world" onwards corresponds to the first phrase.
This may also be explained collectively under the ninth phrase.
From "Having extensively seen the various Buddhas" onwards, the eleventh section clarifies the purity of the roots of goodness;
this is termed the fruit of pliancy (*mṛdu-karmaṇyatā*).
The section beginning with "Having performed much" constitutes the twelfth [section], which consists of three phrases and is called the fruit of the encompassing of dharmas (*dharmasaṃgrahaphala*).
*Suyāma* means "Good Time" (*sukāla*).

In the commentary on the title of this chapter, it says: "The factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), knowing them as they truly are, being able to accomplish the teaching of the True Dharma, and the illumination of wisdom, etc.
Jing states:
"Within the fourth stage, the knowledge of the path-factors (mārgāṅga) cultivated in the practice of the path is called 'flame' (jvālā)."
The wisdom capable of establishing the teaching is called "insight" (prajñā);
it is named the Stage of Blazing Insight (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi). Jiji states:
It is said that the teaching of the True Dharma (saddharma-deśanā) is that which is illuminated;
because this wisdom can illuminate the teaching of the True Dharma, it is called the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
Within the dwelling of superior wisdom (adhiprajñā-vihāra) associated with the various truths (satya), one asks for the resolution of doubts and the severing of fetters.
Within this explanation there are ten points.
First, by cultivating ten kinds of equal intention (*samacittatā*), one enters the fifth stage.
Regarding the statement that its characteristics should be understood as they are taught in the sūtras:
As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:
"O sons of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva in the fifth stage has fully perfected all practices in the fourth bodhisattva stage and wishes to enter the fifth bodhisattva stage..."
One should enter the fifth stage by means of ten kinds of profound, pure, and impartial minds.
What are these ten?
First, because of the profound, pure, and impartial mind regarding the Buddha-dharma of the past.
Second, the future Buddha-dharma;
third, the present Buddha-dharma;
fourth, purity of ethical discipline.
5. Purity of mind;
6. Purity through the removal of views, doubt, and remorse;
7. Purity of knowledge regarding what is the path and what is not the path.
Eighth is the purity of knowledge through the abandonment of the eight modes of conduct.
Ninth is the progressive purity of all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) through thorough investigation.
Tenth is the purity of the mind that is equal and profoundly pure because it brings all sentient beings to maturity.
The treatise says:
The antidote to the pride of superiority consists of the ten kinds of profound and pure equanimity.
Because they share the same thought of non-retrogression,
the antidote to the pride of conceptualizing phenomena was already explained in the preceding stage;

Now, within this ground, it is like a lapis lazuli jewel adorning the gold before; thus,
all grounds should be understood according to the preceding description.
Regarding the "four wind-wheels," these refer to the winds of the four directions.
The phrase "beings who undergo birth mostly [act] as follows" is the tenth [section].
The eleventh sentence can be understood.
Within the "Abiding in the Signless with Application and Effort" (*sābhoga-saprayoga-nimitta-vihāra*), there is an inquiry into the resolution of knots;
within this resolution, there are twelve [points].
First, it is explained that one enters by attaining the fulfillment of the superior practices for progressing on the path, which are introduced by sublime wisdom.
Regarding those who have already attained the ten kinds of sublime skillful means and wisdom:

this wisdom is precisely that which introduces the mundane, uncommon [practices] shared with no other sentient beings, concerning all the superior practices for progressing on the path within all worlds, for the purpose of entering and abiding.
Jing said:
"Because their practice accords with the world, it is called 'common';
because they are not defiled by worldly dharmas, it is called 'uncommon'."
Seeking that stage is called the path of progress;
practicing the conduct of the subsequent stages is called superior practice.
Ji says:
This superior practice of the path of progress is called "mundane" because it involves conditioned activities and possesses distinctions among its objective referents;
it is called "unshared" because it is not bound by the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Because its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*) and because it possesses characteristics, it is also called "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*).
Because it is not something that sentient beings can practice, it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).
Because it performs the function of serving as a condition for phenomena, it is called "shared."
Cai states:
Because wisdom does not abide in saṃsāra, it is called "unshared" (āveṇika);
because compassion does not enter nirvāṇa, it is called "shared."
Regarding the statement that one should know the common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) as explained at length in the sutra:
the *Bhūmi-sūtra* states that when a bodhisattva has fully perfected the practices of the six stages and wishes to enter the seventh stage...
One should enter by means of ten types of skillful means and branches of wisdom that give rise to sublime conduct. What are these ten?
[And so forth, as extensively explained.]
The author of the treatise classifies these ten into four categories:
the first is termed the matter of the causes for the body and wealth;
the second is termed the matter of the causes for guarding against evil.
The third is called the matter of protecting the causes of virtue.
The latter seven are called the matters of the causes for birth by transformation.
Now, regarding what is said here—"namely, relying on that which can give rise to worldly prosperity and the accumulation of merit"—it refers to this.
This means that it refers to the merit encompassed by the bodhisattva practices, which serve as the basis for the causes that give rise to worldly prosperity;
that is, the first matter concerning the cause of physical wealth.
As the Sūtra says: "Because one who skillfully cultivates emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness accumulates great merit that aids the path.
Second is the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
Since many [beings] give rise to malice toward sentient beings,
sentient beings are the cause of evil.
Now, because one directs an altruistic intention (*adhyāśaya*) toward those sentient beings for their benefit and happiness, one does not give rise to evil.
This refers to the protection against unwholesome causes.

As the Sūtra says: "One enters into the selflessness of all phenomena, the absence of a life-principle, and the absence of a sentient being, yet does not abandon the arousal of the four immeasurables.
Third, regarding the basis for the progressive advancement of the accumulations of merit for bodhi and the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
It is for the sake of swiftly accumulating the provisions to realize the fruit of *bodhi*.
This refers to the matter of protecting virtuous causes.
As the Sūtra says: "One gives rise to the dharmas of merit and performs the practice of the supreme *pāramitās*, yet there is no dharma that can be grasped."
The four reliances that are not shared with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are precisely the causal basis for birth by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Among the seven gates, this is the first: taking birth through the power of vows as the primary means to transform and guide other sentient beings.
The Sūtra states that one attains detachment from the three realms while being able to manifest transformative emanations to initiate practices that adorn the three realms.
Fifth, regarding the realm of sentient beings:
this refers to the second section, which explains the application of remedies.
The Sūtra says: "Because ultimate quiescent nirvāṇa can give rise to the practice of nirvāṇa that eliminates greed, hatred, and delusion for the sake of all sentient beings.
Sixth, regarding the reliance upon the dharmadhātu:
This third gate is for the purpose of extinguishing all hindrances.

The Sūtra says: "In accordance with illusions, dreams, echoes, shadows, transformations, the moon in water, and images in a mirror, one gives rise to the mind of immeasurable distinctions within nirvāṇa, based on the non-duality of intrinsic nature."
Regarding the seventh point, "relying upon all worlds":
this is the fourth section, because it concerns the gathering of the great assembly of the Dharma.
As the Sūtra says: "Because they skillfully know that the paths of all lands are like space, they give rise to the practice of adorning and purifying Buddha-lands."
Eighth, regarding the wisdom that relies upon the bodies of all Tathāgatas:
this is the fifth gate, because it generates merit through seeing, hearing, approaching, making offerings to, and practicing in accordance with them.
The Sūtra says: "Knowing that the self-nature of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is bodiless, yet giving rise to the practice of adorning the marks and signs of the form body."
The ninth [point], based on the wisdom of the speech of all Tathāgatas, is because it is the sixth gateway for turning the wheel of Dharma.

The Sūtra says: "Knowing that the voices of all Buddhas are voiceless, originally quiescent, and possess the characteristic of being ineffable, yet they give rise to various distinct and adorned vocalizations in accordance with all sentient beings."
Regarding the tenth point, "relying on the mental wisdom of all Tathāgatas":
this is because it provides an excellent explanation for what was asked in the seventh section.

The Sūtra says: "Entering into the Buddhas, in a single moment of thought, they penetrate the events of the three periods of time and are able to discern their various characteristics; they observe the number of kalpas of practice according to the differences in the minds of all sentient beings."

"Because the bodhisattva is in union with that," and so forth, is the second section, which clarifies the uninterrupted application (*anantarya-prayoga*) arising from the thorough penetration of the Tathāgata’s sphere.
This extends from the beginning up to the phrase "the Tathāgata’s sphere."
This means that because it is conjoined with the ten aforementioned sublime skillful means and wisdoms,
one is able to penetrate the realm of all Tathāgatas;
for the sphere of activity of the aforementioned wisdom is the realm of the Buddhas.
Regarding the statement that for them there arises effortless (*anābhoga*) and signless (*animitta*) [equanimity], up to "not departing from the path," Jing says:
This is because within the eighth stage, true contemplation is effortless.
It is said that there is no effort, no signs, and no conceptualization;
however, conventional observation still involves effort,
as it is able to know that conventional truth is like an illusion or a magical transformation.
Therefore, it is said that there is no differentiated conceptualization.
In the eighth stage, contemplating the realm of those two truths is called "contemplating the immeasurable realm of the Buddhas.
These two contemplations merely give rise to [the realization], which is termed "arising without interval" (*nirantara*).
Observing both the ultimate and the conventional simultaneously is further termed "unimpaired.
Now, in order to give rise to such contemplative practice in the eighth stage,
the bodhisattvas of the seventh stage diligently cultivate and train in all modes of deportment.
Whether walking or standing, one should constantly maintain mental attention;
in all states, one must not be separated from the Path.
Jì (基) says:
Furthermore, for the sake of the Buddha-realm, one gives rise to effortless, signless, and non-conceptually-constructed discrimination,
as well as immeasurable subsequently attained wisdom based on dependent origination;
thus, one contemplates the realm of all Buddhas without interruption.

One should always diligently train in all modes of deportment—whether walking, standing, or acting—so that one's mental attention never departs from mind, speech, and body while performing these actions.
To practice in this way in every state and situation is the path of non-separation.
This effortless, signless contemplation of the Buddha’s realm is the path;
one does not depart from it during any state of activity, whether walking, standing, or attending to mental objects within the modes of conduct.
Therefore, the concluding text below states: "Because they have attained penetration into the realm of the Tathāgata and give rise to uninterrupted and flawless diligent application.

From the phrase "In each and every moment of mind... onwards, the third section clarifies that in each and every *kṣaṇa*, one perfectly realizes all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "In the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva fully possesses all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
However, because the seventh stage is preeminent, it alone receives this name," and so on, as explained at length.
Now, regarding the one who fully initiates all factors of awakening (bodhipākṣika-dharma) that constitute the perfection of all Buddha-dharmas within this very seventh stage:
it is because in each and every thought-moment throughout the seven stages, they constantly give rise to the ten perfections (pāramitā).
Regarding the statement that "the factors of enlightenment are fully endowed and perfected," because this dwelling is subsumed within the perfection of the bodhisattva’s preparatory practices,
it signifies the culmination of effort.
"Wondrous wisdom" refers to the wisdom of skillful means regarding emptiness.
"Purified spiritual powers and conduct" refers to—
It gives rise to the sublime practices of the world;
practicing while free from signs is called purification.
One who is able to enter the eighth stage is [so described].
Upon the completion of the stage of effortful practice, one attains entry into the eighth stage, the state of effortless practice (*anābhoga*).
According to the interpretation of Master Ce and others,

this is because [the seventh stage] is subsumed under the perfection of the bodhisattva’s preparatory practices (*prayoga*) and because it leads to the ability to enter the eighth dwelling (*vihāra*).
This is judged to be the fourth phrase, which is subsumed under "the perfection of the practice with application.
From the passage beginning "Since this bodhisattva... onwards belongs to the fifth phrase.
Now, I shall adopt the Master Jing’s judgment of the text.
Because it accords with the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*),
this dwelling of the bodhisattva is immediately followed by the fourth [chapter], which establishes the defiled and the undefiled.
That is to say, the eighth stage is exclusively pure because it is characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*).
The seventh stage is called "mixed" because it involves effortful application (*sābhoga*).
This seventh stage is called "untainted" because one first attains the signless (*animitta*) here, which serves as the precursor to the eighth stage.

However, because the fundamental signlessness has not yet been attained, there is still effortful application and aspiration; since one is unable to remain spontaneously in the signless, one still falls into the category of the tainted (*saṃkleśa*).
Now, from this point within the present dwelling, the fifth section clarifies the phrases concerning the perfect inclusion of the practice with application (*prayoga*).
As the *Bhūmi-sūtra* states:
"When a bodhisattva dwells in the stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*), they are neither called one who possesses afflictions (*kleśa*) nor called one who is free from afflictions."
Why is this? Because all afflictions do not manifest, they are not called "those with afflictions";
because their seeking of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is not yet fulfilled, they are not called "those without afflictions."
Jingyun: The superior and middle grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation have already been suppressed and rendered inactive during the path of seeing;
however, for the sake of sentient beings, they still arise from the first up to the seventh ground.
Even when lower-grade afflictions manifest again,
it is now said that the primary afflictions such as greed and so forth are all completely severed.

This is based on the fact that during the seventh stage, while one frequently enters meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), the occasions when one emerges from observation and gives rise to delusions are extremely rare.
Because it occurs frequently, it is said that greed and the other [afflictions] are all completely severed. Ji says:
"In this state, all greed and the other [afflictions] are completely severed."
Abiding upon the ground and filling the mind is not severed by the mind of the eighth ground;
this shall be analyzed in due course according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
It should be known that this dwelling is not possessed of afflictions, as the subsequent commentary explains: "It is not possessed of afflictions."
The stage is considered fulfilled because no afflictions manifest.
As previously explained, this does not mean being free from afflictions; the subsequent explanation states:
"One seeks the Buddha-wisdom but has not yet attained it."
Because there remains an attachment to the Buddha’s bodhi that resembles craving, one is not free from afflictions.
Therefore, the concluding text below states: "Because the practice of application is perfected.
From the phrase "The practitioner who... onwards, the sixth section clarifies the purity of the three karmas.
Based on the purity of one's intention, worldly skillful activities proceed and all are brought to perfection;
for this reason, the fulfillment of skillful activities in the seventh stage is specifically elucidated.
Whatever craft or construction is undertaken must necessarily result in functional utility and the accomplishment of its intended purpose.
From the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one studies various crafts for the benefit of sentient beings, seeking wealth and resources in order to practice giving and charity.
The mastery of the crafts studied up to the seventh stage only begins to be perfected at that point,
because it is at the seventh stage that effort reaches its culmination and the crafts become fully accomplished. Thus,
one acts when praised by the Buddha and does not act when not praised.
As explained in the context of the fourth stage,
one has already attained mastery of the arts in the fifth dwelling;
now, upon reaching the seventh stage, this mastery becomes further perfected.
Therefore, the entire trichiliocosm collectively acknowledges him as their teacher.
To be brief, those bodhisattvas at the stage of equality are not mentioned,
because bodhisattvas at the stage of equality do not take one another as teachers.
In the eighth stage, the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth abide like a maturation (*vipāka*), manifesting spontaneously without the need for preparatory effort (*prayoga*);
however, in this present stage, they have not yet become spontaneous.
Because the eighth stage is a state of maturation (*vipākasthiti*), it involves effortful application;
thus, the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth can only manifest when the characteristics of cultivation are present before one.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* differs slightly from this.
Therein, all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are cultivated in the present without receiving the karmic retribution of those dharmas.
This section, following the seventh [chapter], clarifies that these bodhisattvas have attained the samādhis not shared with the two vehicles (*advaya-yāna*).
Regarding "such skillful means up to the gates of samādhi," the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"The bodhisattva dwelling in the seventh stage enters the bodhisattva-samādhi named 'Wisdom of Excellent Discernment,' and so forth."
In this way, the Bodhisattva, having fulfilled these thirteen foremost samādhis which are gateways of such great wisdom and supernormal power,
is able to enter hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva samādhi-gateways and thoroughly purify this stage.
The *Old Treatise* states:
"In this dwelling, the bodhisattva contemplates skillful means and enters the Samādhi of Skillful Subjugation (*suvilīna*),
giving rise to one million samādhis."
Regarding the statement, "The Bodhisattva thus remains entirely remote from all afflictions, even up to the point of courageous application of effort," Jing says:
"Because the Bodhisattva of the seventh stage is free from all delusions, the three karmas accompanied by all conceptual constructions no longer function at all."
Yet they do not abandon the courageous application of seeking awakening.
Ki says: "Because there is subtle conceptualization, it is difficult to discern."
Because it is free from coarse conceptualization, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).
In the preceding stages, there is coarse conceptualization, which is termed "with signs" (*sanimitta*);
however, because these [conceptualizations] all accord with enlightenment, they are not abandoned.
That which is manifested by the skillful cultivation of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) means that one enters deeply into true contemplation,
whereby the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena increases and becomes clearer with every thought-moment; therefore,
it is said that one has skillfully cultivated the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
The patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the direct realization of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Furthermore, among the various bodhisattvas, this eighth stage clarifies the ability to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in every moment of thought.
While the absorption of cessation entered during the sixth stage was previously mentioned, here, within this [eighth] stage, one is able to enter it in every moment of thought.
Master Jing said:
"To speak only of the sixth dwelling and not the preceding five dwellings is to indicate the beginning by citing the end."

From the first stage through the sixth, there is the distinction of entering and emerging from meditative absorption because the state of cessation is not constant; thus, the sixth stage is specifically mentioned.
By this analogy, it is shown that the preceding five stages also involve temporary entry into cessation.
Alternatively, one may consider that the first three stages are identical to the mundane world and do not concern the attainment of that cessation.
The fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are the same as those of the Two Vehicles.

In the first stage, one initially attains the untainted factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*), which is analogous to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) who has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

In the fifth stage, the Bodhisattva is like one at the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*) who likewise has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation; for this reason, it is not discussed here.

The Bodhisattva of the sixth stage is discussed specifically because he attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), which is characteristic of one who has attained the third fruit [of the śrāvaka path].

The Bodhisattva of the seventh stage attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) like an arhat, and thus enters the meditative absorption of cessation in every moment of thought.
Question: If one enters cessation in every moment throughout the seven stages, then the two types of wisdom would ultimately not function.
Answer: This is based on the capacity to enter cessation in every moment.
It is not necessarily the case that one enters cessation in every moment of thought.
However, if one relies on the true contemplation that is free from characteristics— the conventional designation for "cessation"—
then one enters it in every moment of thought.
The Tripitaka Master says:
There are two interpretations in the West.
One states:
Only from the eighth stage upward do they enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);
Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage and below who have attained sudden enlightenment cannot enter it. Why is this so?
From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onward, because the afflictions of the three realms have been transcended yet remain manifest, one cannot enter [this samādhi].
As for the statement that one can enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) during the sixth and seventh stages:

it is based on the fact that this is called the "absorption of cessation" because it accords with the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and takes the quiescence of all conditioned phenomena as its object.
It is not the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) among the twenty-four dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
One view states that from the first bhūmi upward, all enter the attainment of cessation.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Mahāmati,
"From the first stage up to the sixth stage, one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)."
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also enter the meditative absorption of cessation;
yet, at times, even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to enter it.
Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage enter the meditative absorption of cessation in every moment of thought.
Regarding the statement that one enters the sixth bhūmi now:
because one attains the signless (*animitta*) within the sixth bhūmi, one is able to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Being able to subdue the afflictions, one is able to break through and enter the obstacle to the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master says:
from the sixth bhūmi downwards, one enters the samāpatti of cessation only after performing immeasurable preparatory applications;
in the seventh bhūmi, however, one enters it immediately upon the desire to do so through skillful means.
Therefore, it is provisionally stated that one enters [the state] moment by moment;
this does not mean that the term "moment by moment" refers to the meaning of a continuous succession.
The reason for this is as follows:
This is because from the sixth bhūmi downwards, there is also entry into [meditative absorption] through a succession of many moments.
Nevertheless, this bodhisattva’s extremely rare and marvelous feat consists in being able to reach this state without realizing it.
This further clarifies that Bodhisattvas on the seventh stage constantly enter the realm of the true contemplation of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
yet do not realize it [as a final cessation] in order to initiate practices for the benefit of others.
From "By means of such as these" below, the ninth section explains the manifestation of conduct that is uncommon to all sentient beings and the world.
Jingyun: It is called "unshared" because it is able to perform all actions identical to those of sentient beings, yet differs from the sublime practices performed by bodhisattvas.
Although the sublime practices of bodhisattvas are similar to those of the world, they do not share the same nature as that of the world.
As explained at length in the sutra, Cè states:
"Although he dwells amidst defilement, he remains unstained by it; therefore, it is called 'unshared' (asādhāraṇa)."
The general meaning herein is set forth below as it appears in the sūtra cited, showing that their conduct is similar to that of ordinary sentient beings.
There are eight points in this general meaning:
first, the commonality of meritorious deeds.
Second, they are identical in gathering in kinsmen and followers;
third, they are identical in seeking rebirth as ordinary beings;
fourth, they are identical with those who have first resolved their minds in initiating the pursuit of abiding in the three gates of liberation.
5. The matter of sharing the same faith and delight in the Lesser Vehicle for the sake of disciplining others;
6. The matter of sharing the same enjoyment of various sensual desires;
7. The matter of turning away from non-Buddhists toward the Buddha.
The eighth [point] is that he conforms to the minds of others and conforms to the masses like worldly people;
the remainder is as previously explained. Below, the tenth [point] clarifies the purity of the roots of goodness.
From "In his births, he mostly acts as... onwards, the textual characteristics of the eleventh and twelfth [points], concerning the power of his births, are clear to understand.
Master Ji says:
These twelve sections within this ground should be understood by correlating them according to their respective structures.
Regarding the fifth, it is because it is subsumed under the perfection of preparatory practice (*prayoga*).
Looking at the preceding text, it appears to be connected with the fourth inversion;
the fourth is combined with the fifth,
and the fifth is combined within the fourth.
The Tripitaka Master says:
"This fifth [stage], characterized by the perfection of preparatory practice (*prayoga*),
refers to the complete eradication of all greed and other afflictions within this present dwelling."
Because the practice with application (*sābhoga-prayoga*) has been perfected, one thereby abandons the remaining afflictions;
this is still the sequential binding of non-inverted dharmas.
Within the state of dwelling in signlessness without application (*anābhoga-nimitta-vihāra*), the question is resolved regarding the binding.
Within this explanation, there are eleven [sections].
First is the clarification of entering the fulfillment of the wisdom that realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena.
According to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, it is said:
First, all dharmas are fundamentally unborn;
second, they are unestablished;
third, they are signless.
Fourth, non-emergence;
fifth, non-commonality;
sixth, inexhaustibility.
Seventh, non-activity.
Eighth, the absence of the nature of existence.
Ninth, equality in the beginning, middle, and end.
The ten suchnesses are entered into non-conceptually through the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The Commentary explains that this patience (*kṣānti*) should be understood in terms of four kinds of non-arising (*anutpāda*):
first, the non-arising of things (*vastu*).
Second, the non-arising of intrinsic nature;
third, the non-arising of numerical distinctions;
fourth, the non-arising of distinctions in activity.
The first seven phrases concern the non-arising of phenomena;
the latter three correspond, respectively, to the final three types of non-arising.
As Master Yuan and others have explained:
There are ten phrases concerning the non-arising of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-anutpāda*).
The wisdom that understands this non-arising is called "entry-wisdom" (*praveśajñāna*).
Now, I shall further speak of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena.
This refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested by the removal of the two types of grasping.
Now, it is clarified that the removal of the two types of grasping and the *tathatā* thus manifested is called "the wisdom that enters the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena.
Based on the three times, as appropriate, ten kinds [of this wisdom] are set forth below.
Jingyun: This differs slightly from the text of the *Daśabhūmika*,
though its general meaning is similar.
Ji says: "As in the text of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
this may be a distinct interpretation by the commentator."
The current text does not fully set forth these ten dharmas.
These ten dharmas refer to the three times as they correspond;
that is, because such conceptual attachments exist according to the three times, they are presented here as appropriate.
These ten [aspects] all exclude the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The ten phrases, such as "originally unborn," are to be applied respectively.
This is explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Dì jīng).
Master Yuan said:
"Regarding 'those of the three periods,' this refers to the first seven stages as the past in relation to the eighth stage."
The first stage is named "the present," while the remaining two stages are named "the future. Among these,
the first four should be assigned to the three periods of time.
What is the meaning of this?
Regarding the past, there are the first two, namely non-arising and non-origination;
regarding the present, it is signlessness.
The future has no establishment;
the past is divided into two;
the first stage is called "arising."
The stages from the second to the seventh are called "arising.
"Non-arising" refers to the absence of the arising of the pure dharmas of the first stage;
"non-origination" refers to the absence of origination from the second stage onward.
"Arising" refers to the act of arising;
these two terms exclude the calculation of the past.
As for "signlessness":
One clings to the notion that the eighth stage possesses the characteristic of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
now, by removing this clinging to characteristics, one speaks of "signlessness" (*animitta*),
which is precisely the present.
Regarding the statement "non-attainment":
this refers to the absence of anything from the ninth stage upward up until the attainment of Buddhahood and bodhi;
yet, there is still this clinging to such Buddhahood and bodhi.
Now, these are eliminated together.
According to the old treatise, there are only these four;
the latter three types do not exist.
There are three further types.
[Daoshi] says:
"According to the examination of the Sanskrit original of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* by the Tripiṭaka Master, there are ten kinds of contemplation on non-arising (*anutpāda-darśana*)."
First, non-arising;
second, non-origination;
third, signlessness.
Fourth, there is no establishment.
Fifth, there is no loss.
Sixth, there is no existence of an intrinsic nature.
7. The nature of non-transmigration;
8. The nature of non-cessation;
9. The nature of equality in the beginning, middle, and end.
Tenth, there is the non-conceptual equality of entering into suchness without inversion.
These ten types are identical to those found in the original version of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the commentary on the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.
In the ten phrases of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the first five are entirely identical [to those here].
There is no sixth phrase, "the nature of existence does not exist.
The two phrases "no coming and no going" correspond here to the "nature of non-transmigration" and the "nature of non-cessation."
"Without beginning, middle, or end"—this single phrase is also as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
That treatise states:

3. The Third Section on the Ultimate Yoga: The Chapter on Birth within the Section on the Ultimate Yoga. (12a) Regarding the first chapter, "Birth," this constitutes the third of the four sections of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

Because one attains the ultimate through the preceding essential requirements and thereby encompasses the benefit of both self and others, it is called the "Ultimate Yoga Station" (*niṣṭhā-yoga-sthāna*).
It consists of five chapters;
as it encompasses the arising [of beings] at the outset, it is called the first.
Within these five categories,

Thereafter, there is one chapter that distinguishes the fruits in relation to the practices.
Within the preceding [section], there are two parts;

The final chapter distinguishes the stages upon which the practices depend.
